rationale: A wins because it keeps the ClassPass temptation in the right place: as an uncomfortable question, not a fabricated story. A's "Mindbody bundles its AI assistant into existing plans, skipping the AI surcharge" turns a supplied pricing fact into a real SaaS-business angle with proof gates; B's "now its AI sits on top of both" leaps past the evidence and sells a platform-power story before proving the products touch. B has usable bones, but that headline writes a check the facts cannot cash.
gaps_in_A: "most boutique studios will never buy an AI tool" is unsupported by the update; A should frame that as a hypothesis requiring evidence, not a fact.
"The prevailing pattern that reporter is tracking is AI as a paid add-on or premium tier" needs comparator proof; A asks for it later, but the angle still leans on an outside market claim.
"What happened when a studio let an AI text its waitlist" is useful but conditional; without the named pilot studio A says it needs, this is not pitch-ready.
gaps_in_B: "now its AI sits on top of both" is not in the supplied facts; the update does not say the assistant interacts with ClassPass inventory.
"using aggregated booking data across the network" invents scope. The update says booking data, not network-wide aggregated data.
"software decides the schedule" overstates the fact. The update says the assistant suggests optimal class times, which is a weaker and more accurate claim.
B misses the clean pricing story: "pricing is bundled into existing software tiers" could support a monetization/AI-surcharge angle, while B spends that slot on speculative ClassPass platform power.
